summary: Proposes a suspend and resume solution for the real-time encapsulation part of the same architecture, letting urgent PPP frames interrupt a long one.

eli5.summary: Pause a long message mid-sentence to say an urgent thing, then resume the long one.

questions: what is the fse byte in ppp
how does ppp suspend and resume packets
why do real time packets need ppp framing
subtitle: How to let an urgent real-time packet cut in line on a slow PPP link by pausing and resuming a long one.

tldr.problem: On a slow link such as a 28.8 kbit/s modem, a single 1500 byte packet blocks the line for about 400 ms, which makes real-time conversation unusable.
tldr.mechanism: It adds a compact PPP multilink fragment header plus a real-time frame format in which a special fragment suspend escape byte (FSE, 0xDE) lets a sender stop a packet at any point, send urgent data and resume later.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard for the suspend/resume part of an architecture for integrated services over low-bitrate links; its metadata lists no replacement.

today: RFC 2687 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the suspend/resume-oriented option for the real-time encapsulation part of the architecture in RFC 2689.

sections.title: The Delay Problem on Slow Links
sections.content:
This RFC is one piece of an architecture for carrying real-time multimedia, called integrated services, over low-bitrate links such as modem lines, ISDN B-channels and sub-T1 links. Its piece is the real-time encapsulation format: how packets are framed on the wire.

The motivation is simple arithmetic. A 1500 byte packet on a 28.8 kbit/s modem link keeps the link unavailable for real-time data for about 400 ms. That adds a worst-case delay that pushes round-trip times to at least a second, which is unacceptable for real-time conversation.

The document takes the suspend/resume approach. A true suspend/resume design can only be implemented on a type-1 sender, but it gives that sender the best possible delay. Type-1 and type-2 receivers can both implement the format. The RFC builds on RFC 1990 (PPP Multilink) and RFC 2686 (its multi-class extension).
sections.eli5: A big packet on a slow line is like a very long truck on a narrow road. Everyone behind it has to wait, and a phone call cannot wait that long.

sections.title: General Approach and Requirements
sections.content:
The requirements follow those of RFC 2686: predictability, robustness, and cooperation with PPP and existing hardware and firmware, including async-to-sync converters. A suspend/resume design can give better worst-case latency than the pre-fragmenting design of that RFC, and since it needs a new encapsulation anyway, it can also be a little more efficient. Operation over multiple links is only a partial non-requirement: the format is based on PPP Multilink, but many uses involve a single link.

Plain multilink is a poor fit for suspension. The "end" bit sits in the multilink header, which is the wrong place for suspend/resume. A suspendable packet has to be sent with the end bit off and usually closed later with an empty fragment, so the minimum overhead is twice the multilink header size (six bytes, including a compressed multilink protocol field) plus one PPP framing of three bytes. Each suspension costs another six bytes.

The RFC therefore introduces two new features: a compact fragment format and header, and a real-time frame format.
sections.eli5: The old way needed a long label on every piece, like writing a full address on each page of a letter. This RFC shortens the label so pausing costs less.

sections.title: Compact and Extended Fragment Headers
sections.content:
The compact fragment format is an optional multilink fragment format tuned for single-link use and frequent suspension. Its header is one octet: an R bit, a three-bit sequence number, a three-bit class field, and a least significant bit that is always 1. That last bit helps HDLC chips that treat the least significant bit of an address specially. The multilink protocol identifier is not sent at all, which needs prior negotiation, as with address and control field compression.

The R bit is the inverse of the multilink B bit: R = 1 means this fragment resumes a packet that has already been started. If the class field is 7, R MUST never be 1, so class 7 frames cannot be suspended. This also avoids a header byte of 0xFF, which would be confused with the start of an LCP negotiation.

When the class field is 7 the sequence field is free, so it selects eight more classes. The effective class number is 0 to 6 for class fields 0 to 6, and 7 to 14 for class field 7. Classes 0 to 6 are suspendable; classes 7 to 14 are for non-suspendable high-priority traffic such as highly compressed voice streams.

For multiple links, a three-bit sequence number is rarely enough, so an optional extended compact fragment format uses two octets. The first octet holds R, the three least significant sequence bits, the class and a 0 in the last bit. The second octet holds seven more sequence bits and ends in a 1. Each fragment says which format it uses, and one of the two formats SHOULD be used consistently within each suspendable class.
sections.eli5: The label on each piece is squeezed into one small byte: is this a continuation, which piece number, and how urgent. A longer two-byte label exists for when many roads are used.

sections.title: The Real-Time Frame and the FSE Byte
sections.content:
The real-time frame keeps the usual HDLC-like frame so existing synchronous HDLC chips and async-to-sync converters still work. The missing piece is the multilink E bit, which says a fragment is the last of its packet. Here the end of a normal frame implicitly means E = 1, so a finished packet triggers a receive interrupt even on type-2 receivers.

A fragment that is being suspended ends inside the frame with a special fragment suspend escape byte, FSE, whose value is 0xDE. Everything before the last FSE counts as suspended (E = 0). A frame may even end with an FSE, meaning its last fragment is suspended and no final fragment follows. Each fragment starts with its own compact header. The scheme does not apply to frames that start with 0xFF, the standard PPP address field, and an implementation MUST NOT request both address and control field compression and this format.

Data transparency is the catch: real data can contain 0xDE. After an FSE the receiver expects a header, and a class 7 header with R = 1 is reserved. So an FSE followed by one of 0x8F, 0x9F up to 0xFF is special. The high four bits of that second byte tell the receiver where to re-insert FSE bytes that were removed from the data. For example 0x8F means insert one FSE and go back to data, and 0xFF means insert four FSE bytes. The worst-case expansion from this is about 25 %, and a data stream can trigger worst-case FSE expansion or worst-case octet or bit stuffing, but never both.
sections.eli5: A special marker byte means "pausing here". If the real message happens to contain that marker, a small code after it tells the receiver to put the markers back, like spelling out a word that would otherwise be mistaken for a command.

sections.title: Implementation Notes
sections.content:
Two practical points are covered. First, the LCP maximum receive unit (MRU) limits packet size, and async-to-sync converters watching LCP may treat it as the largest HDLC frame to expect. Implementations should preferably negotiate an MRU big enough for the worst-case 25 % growth plus the growth from suspended fragments. If that is not possible, the sender should watch frame sizes and suspend the current fragment by sending an FSE followed by an empty final fragment, then continue in a new HDLC frame. That also limits the effect of longer frames on the safety of the 16-bit FCS.

Second, the simplest implementation does normal HDLC processing first and FSE processing on the result. A combined automaton must wait until two bytes are available and a third has followed, so the final FCS bytes are not mistaken for data.
sections.eli5: If the road has a height limit, keep the load small enough to fit, or split it into two trips.

sections.title: Negotiating the Format
sections.content:
Negotiation reuses options from PPP Multilink (maximum received reconstructed unit, short sequence number header format, endpoint discriminator) and from the multi-class extension (multilink header format, prefix elision). This RFC adds two new code points to the Multilink Header Format option, which is LCP option type 27 with length 4, a code byte and a count of suspendable classes.

Code 11 means the basic and extended compact real-time fragment format with classes in an FSE-encoded HDLC frame. Code 15 means the basic compact format only. The negotiated class limit only restricts suspendable class numbers; classes 7 and higher need no extra reassembly space and are not subject to it.
sections.eli5: Before talking, both ends agree which kind of shortened label they will use, like choosing a secret handshake.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says operation is believed to be no more and no less secure than PPP Multilink. One difference comes from the small sequence number range: fragments from different packets could be wrongly reassembled into one packet. Most such packets would be discarded because of higher-layer checksum failures, but contents of packets for one host could be delivered to another. Links where this matters SHOULD use the extended sequence number range for multi-fragment packets.
sections.eli5: With very short page numbers, pages from two letters could get shuffled together. Using longer page numbers makes mix-ups much less likely.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: 1 means this fragment resumes a packet already started.

fields.name: Sequence
fields.desc: Three-bit sequence number used for loss detection.

fields.name: Class
fields.desc: Class 0 to 6, or 7 for the extra classes 7 to 14.
